title: Book 4
paragraphs: For nine years — from my nineteenth year to my twenty-eighth — we lived seduced and seducing others, deceived and deceiving others, caught up in every kind of desire: openly, through the subjects they call the liberal arts; secretly, under a religion that wore a false name. Proud here, superstitious there, empty everywhere. Here, chasing after the emptiness of popular applause — down to theater ovations, poetry contests, competitions for garlands of grass, the foolishness of public shows, and desires with no restraint. There, wanting to be washed clean of these same stains, by carrying food to the men they called "the elect" and "the holy" — food out of which, in the factory of their stomachs, they would manufacture for us angels and gods who would cleanse us. These were the things I pursued and practiced with my friends, who were deceived by me and deceived along with me. Let the arrogant laugh at me, and those who have not, for the health of their souls, been struck down and humbled by you, my God — but I will still confess my own shame to you, for your praise. Allow me, I beg you, grant me the grace to go back now in memory over the wanderings of my past, and to offer you the sacrifice of thanksgiving. For what am I to myself without you, but a guide leading myself to ruin? Or what am I, even at my best, but an infant sucking the milk you give, feeding on you, the food that never perishes? But what kind of man is any man, given that he is only a man? Let the strong and the powerful laugh at us now — but let us, the poor and the needy, confess to you.

In those years I taught rhetoric, and, conquered by greed, sold a skill in talking meant to conquer others. Yet I preferred — Lord, you know it — honest students, so called, and I taught these tricks of the trade without any trickery of my own, tricks not meant to be used against an innocent person's life, though sometimes meant to be used for a guilty person's life. And you, God, saw me from far off, stumbling on that slippery path, and amid a great deal of smoke you saw a few sparks of good faith, which I showed in the way I guided people who loved emptiness and chased after lies — I was their companion in it. In those years I had one woman — not in what is called lawful marriage, but one I had found through a wandering passion empty of sense — yet only one, and I stayed faithful to her. In my own case with her I learned what difference there is between the restraint of a marriage covenant, entered for the sake of children, and the bargain of a lustful love, where children are born against their parents' will, even though, once born, they force us to love them.

I also remember that when I had decided to compete for a theatrical prize, some sorcerer asked me what I would give him to win. But I, hating and detesting such filthy rites, answered: "Even if the garland were made of gold that never perished, I would not let a fly be killed to win it for me." For he meant to kill living creatures in his sacrifices, and through those offerings invite demons to favor me. But I rejected this evil too, not out of a pure love for you, God of my heart — for I did not know how to love you, since I knew of nothing beyond a kind of physical brightness. And doesn't a soul that sighs after such fictions commit fornication against you, put its trust in things that are not real, and feed the wind? Still, I would not have had sacrifices offered to demons on my behalf — even while I was sacrificing myself to those same demons through my superstition. For what else is it to feed the wind, but to feed them — that is, by going astray, to become their entertainment and their mockery?

As for those frauds people call astrologers — "mathematicians," as they were known — I consulted them without a second thought, because they seemed to use no sacrifice and to pray to no spirit for their predictions. Yet Christian and true piety consistently rejects and condemns that art. For it is a good thing to confess to you and say: have mercy on me, heal my soul, for I have sinned against you; and not to abuse your mercy as license to keep sinning, but to remember the Lord's words: see, you are made well, sin no more, in case something worse happens to you. All this sound advice, astrologers work hard to destroy, saying: "The cause of your sin is fixed unavoidably in the heavens," and "Venus did this, or Saturn, or Mars" — so that man, mere flesh and blood, proud corruption that he is, might be blameless, while the Creator and orderer of the heavens and the stars bears the blame instead. And who is this but our God — the very sweetness and wellspring of righteousness, who repays every man according to his deeds, and will not despise a broken and contrite heart?

In those days there was a wise man, highly skilled in medicine and renowned for it, who — acting in his role as proconsul — had placed the contest garland on my fevered head with his own hand, though not as a physician that time. For this disease only you can cure, you who resist the proud and give grace to the humble. But did you fail me even through that old man, or hold back from healing my soul? For as I got to know him better, and hung closely and constantly on his conversation — which, though plainly spoken, was lively, vigorous, and earnest — he gathered from what I said that I was devoted to books of horoscope-casting, and he advised me kindly, like a father, to throw them away, and not to waste on such vanities the care and diligence that useful things required. He told me that in his younger years he had studied that art so thoroughly he meant to make his living by it, and that, understanding Hippocrates as he did, he could easily have mastered a study like this one — yet he had given it up and turned to medicine instead, for no reason except that he had found it entirely false, and, being a serious man, he would not make his living deceiving people. "But you," he said, "have rhetoric to support yourself with, so that you pursue this out of free choice, not necessity. All the more reason, then, to trust me on this, since I worked to master it so completely that I could have lived by it alone." When I asked him how, then, could so many true things be predicted by it, he answered as best he could, that the force of chance, spread throughout the whole order of things, brought this about. "For if a man opens the pages of some poet at random, a poet who sang and thought of something entirely different, a line often turns up remarkably fitting to the matter at hand — it should be no surprise if, out of the human soul, without the soul itself knowing what is happening within it, some higher instinct produces an answer, by chance and not by skill, that corresponds to the business and actions of the person asking."

And this much you conveyed to me, either from him or through him, and traced it in my memory, so that I might examine it for myself later. But at that time, neither he, nor my dearest Nebridius — a young man of unusual goodness and holy fear, who mocked the whole business of divination — could persuade me to give it up. The authority of the writers on the subject swayed me more, and I had not yet found the certain proof I was looking for, the kind that would show beyond any doubt that what had been truly foretold by those consulted was the result of chance and not of the astrologers' art.

In those years, when I first began teaching rhetoric in my hometown, I had made a friend — too dear to me — through our shared pursuits, a man my own age, in the first flower of youth just as I was. He had grown up with me since childhood; we had been schoolmates and playmates together. But he was not yet my friend in the way he later became, nor even then in the way true friendship is — for friendship cannot be true unless you bind souls together, souls clinging to you through the love poured into our hearts by the Holy Spirit, which is given to us. Still, it was a friendship too sweet, ripened by the warmth of shared studies: for I had twisted him too, away from the true faith — which as a young man he had not taken in soundly or thoroughly — into those superstitious and destructive fables my mother grieved over me for following. His mind now wandered astray with mine, and my soul could not do without him. But look — you were close on the heels of your runaways, God of vengeance and fountain of mercies both at once, turning us back to yourself by wonderful means. You took that man out of this life when he had barely filled a single year of friendship with me, a friendship sweeter to me than anything else sweet in my life at that time.

Who can recount all your praises, which one single man felt within himself? What did you do then, my God, and how unfathomable is the depth of your judgments? For a long time, badly sick with a fever, he lay unconscious in a death-sweat, and when his recovery was given up as hopeless, he was baptized without knowing it — while I, meanwhile, paid little attention, assuming his soul would keep what it had received from me rather than what had been done to his unconscious body. But it turned out very differently: he grew better and recovered. As soon as I could speak with him — and I could, as soon as he was able, for I never left his side, and we depended on each other far too much — I tried to joke with him, assuming he would joke back with me about the baptism he had received while completely absent in mind and feeling, but had now come to understand he had received. But he pulled away from me as if I were an enemy, and with a startling, sudden boldness, told me, if I wanted to remain his friend, to stop talking to him that way. Astonished and stunned, I held back all my feelings until he should grow well and his strength be enough for me to deal with him as I wished. But he was taken from my madness, so that he might be kept safe with you for my comfort. A few days later, while I was away, the fever seized him again, and he died.

At this grief my heart went utterly dark, and everything I looked at was death. My hometown was a torment to me, my father's house a strange kind of misery, and everything I had shared with him, now that he was gone, turned into a torture that tore at my mind. My eyes searched for him everywhere, but he was not to be found; and I hated every place, because none of them had him — none of them could tell me any more, "he's coming," the way they could when he was alive and simply away. I became a great riddle to myself, and I asked my own soul why she was so sad, and why she troubled me so deeply — but she had no answer to give me. And if I said, trust in God, she quite rightly did not obey me, because that dearest friend she had lost was, being a man, both truer and better than the phantom she was being told to trust in. Only tears were sweet to me — they took my friend's place, among the things dearest to my heart.

And now, Lord, these things are past, and time has eased my wound. Let me learn from you, who are Truth, and put the ear of my heart close to your mouth — will you tell me why weeping is sweet to the miserable? Have you, though present everywhere, thrown our misery far away from yourself? You abide within yourself, while we are tossed about among all sorts of trials — and yet, unless we mourned in your hearing, we would have no hope left. So where does the sweet fruit come from, gathered out of the bitterness of life, out of groaning, tears, sighs, and complaints? Is it sweetened by our hoping that you hear us? That is true of prayer, since prayer holds a longing to reach you. But is it also true of grief for something lost, the sorrow that overwhelmed me then? For I did not hope he would come back to life, nor did I want that with my tears — I simply wept and grieved. I was miserable, and I had lost my joy. Or is weeping itself actually a bitter thing, and is it out of sheer disgust with the things we used to enjoy that, when we pull back from them, it pleases us?

But why do I keep talking about these things? Now is not the time for questioning, but for confessing to you. I was wretched — and every soul bound by love to things that perish is wretched: it is torn apart when it loses them, and only then feels the wretchedness it already had before losing them. So it was with me then; I wept most bitterly, and found my rest in bitterness. That is how wretched I was, and I held that wretched life dearer than my friend. For though I would gladly have changed it, I was more unwilling to give it up than to give him up — I don't even know whether I would have given it up for him, as is told (if it isn't a fiction) of Pylades and Orestes, that they would gladly have died for each other or together, since not living together was worse to them than death. But in me some unexplained feeling had risen up, quite the opposite of that: I intensely hated to live, and at the same time feared to die. I suppose the more I loved him, the more I hated and feared, as a most cruel enemy, the death that had robbed me of him — and I imagined it would soon put an end to everyone, since it had had power over him. That is how it was with me, I remember. Look at my heart, my God, look and see into me — for I remember it well, my Hope, you who cleanse me from the impurity of such attachments, turning my eyes toward you, and pulling my feet out of the trap. For I was amazed that other men, subject to death, still lived, when he whom I loved as though he would never die, was dead. And I was even more amazed that I myself, who had been a second self to him, could go on living now that he was dead. Someone said well of his own friend, "you, half of my soul" — for I felt that my soul and his soul were one soul in two bodies. And so my life was a horror to me, because I did not want to live halved. And perhaps that is why I feared to die — so that he whom I had loved so much would not die completely.

What madness, not knowing how to love human beings the way human beings should be loved! What a fool I was then, unable to bear patiently the common lot of man! I fretted, sighed, wept, fell apart; I had neither rest nor counsel. For I carried around a shattered, bleeding soul, one that couldn't stand being carried by me, and yet I could find nowhere to set it down and let it rest. Not in calm groves, not in games or music, not in fragrant places, not in elaborate banquets, not in the pleasures of bed and couch — not even, finally, in books or poetry did it find rest. Everything looked ghastly, even the light itself; whatever was not him was hateful and revolting, except groaning and tears — in those alone I found a little relief. But whenever my soul was drawn away from them, a huge weight of misery pressed down on me. That weight should have been lifted up to you, Lord, for you to lighten — I knew this — but I neither could nor would, all the more because, when I thought of you, you were not to me anything solid or substantial. For it was not really you, but a mere phantom, and my error was my god. If I tried to set my burden down on it so it might rest, it slid through the emptiness and came crashing back down on me, and I was left to myself as a wretched place where I could neither stay nor leave. For where could my heart flee from my heart? Where could I flee from myself? Where would I not still be following myself? And yet I fled my own country — for that way my eyes would look for him less, where they were not used to seeing him. And so I left Thagaste and came to Carthage.

Time wastes no time; it does not roll by idly — through our senses it works strange changes on the mind. Look, the days came and went one after another, and by their coming and going brought new thoughts and new memories into my mind, and little by little patched me back together with my old kind of pleasures, to which my grief gradually gave way. And yet what followed were not, it's true, other griefs, but the causes of other griefs. For where had that earlier grief so easily reached down into the very depths of my soul, if not from my having poured out my soul on the dust, loving someone who had to die as though he would never die? What restored and refreshed me most of all was the comfort of other friends, with whom I loved what I loved instead of you — and this was a great fable, a long-drawn-out lie, whose adulterous stimulation defiled our soul, which lay there itching in our ears. But that fable would not die for me, no matter how many of my friends died. There were other things about them that took hold of my mind more: talking and joking together, doing each other kindnesses in turn, reading pleasant books together, playing the fool together or being serious together, disagreeing now and then without any hard feelings, the way one might disagree with oneself, and even seasoning our more frequent agreements with the rare taste of these disagreements; sometimes teaching, sometimes learning; missing those who were absent with impatience, and welcoming those who arrived with joy. These and similar expressions, coming from the hearts of those who loved and were loved in return, through the face, the voice, the eyes, and a thousand pleasing gestures, were so much fuel to melt our souls together and make one out of many.

This is what is loved in friends, and loved so much that a man's own conscience condemns him if he does not love in return someone who loves him, or does not love back someone who loves him, wanting nothing from the other person except signs of their love. Hence that mourning, when one of them dies, and the darkening of sorrows, the heart steeped in tears, all sweetness turned to bitterness; and out of the loss of life in the one who is dying comes the death of the one still living. Blessed is whoever loves you, and loves his friend in you, and his enemy for your sake. For he alone loses no one dear to him, who holds everyone dear in the one who cannot be lost. And who is this but our God, the God who made heaven and earth, and fills them, because by filling them he created them? No one loses you except by leaving you. And whoever leaves you — where does he go, where does he flee, except from you in your kindness to you in your anger? For where does he not find your law in his own punishment? And your law is truth, and you are truth.

Turn us, God of hosts, show us your face, and we will be whole. For wherever the soul of man turns, unless it is toward you, it gets nailed down onto sorrows — even when it is nailed onto beautiful things. And yet those beautiful things, apart from you and apart from the soul, would not exist at all, unless they came from you. They rise and they set; and by rising they begin, in a sense, to exist; they grow, so that they may reach completion; and once complete, they grow old and wither — and while not all of them grow old, all of them wither. So then, when they rise and move toward existing, the more quickly they grow in order to exist, the more quickly they also rush toward not existing. This is the law that governs them. This much you have allotted to them, because they are portions of things which do not all exist at once, but by passing away and following one another, they together make up the whole universe of which they are parts. And in just this way our speech, too, is made complete by sounds that signify: but even this is not complete unless one word passes away, once it has sounded its part, so that another can follow. Out of all these things let my soul praise you, God, Creator of everything — but let my soul not be glued down to these things by love, through the senses of the body. For they go where they were always going, toward not existing, and they tear the soul apart with poisonous longings, because the soul longs to exist, yet loves to find rest in what it loves. But in these things there is no place to rest; they do not stay, they flee — and who can keep up with them using the senses of the flesh? Who can even grasp them while they are right there beside us? For the sense of the flesh is slow, because it is the sense of the flesh, and that is its limit. It is enough for what it was made for, but it is not enough to hold in place things running their course from their appointed starting point to their appointed end. For in your Word, by which they are created, they hear their decree: "from here to there."

Do not be foolish, my soul, and do not go deaf in the ear of your heart from the noise of your own foolishness. Listen, you too. The Word itself calls you to return, and there is the place of unshakeable rest, where love is not abandoned, if it does not abandon itself. Look, these things pass away so that others can take their place, and so this lower universe is completed in all its parts. "But do I go away anywhere?" says the Word of God. Fix your dwelling there, trust there whatever you have from that source, my soul — at least now that you are worn out with vanities. Entrust to the Truth whatever you have from the Truth, and you will lose nothing; and your decay will bloom again, and all your sicknesses will be healed, and your mortal parts will be reshaped and renewed and bound fast around you. They will not lay you down where they themselves descend, but they will stand firm with you and remain forever before God, who abides and stands firm forever.

Why then be perverted and follow your flesh? Let it be converted instead, and follow you. Whatever you sense through the flesh is only a part, and you do not know the whole of which these are parts; and yet they delight you. But if the sense of your flesh had the capacity to grasp the whole, and had not itself also, as your punishment, been justly confined to a part of the whole, you would want whatever exists right now to pass away, so that the whole might please you more. For even what we are speaking now, you hear through that same sense of the flesh — yet you would not want the syllables to stay put; you want them to fly away, so that others may come, and you may hear the whole. And so it always is: when any one thing is made up of many parts that do not all exist at the same time, the whole together would please more than the parts do separately, if only the whole could be perceived all at once. But far better than all these things is he who made them all; and he is our God, and he does not pass away, for nothing succeeds him either.

If bodies please you, praise God because of them, and turn your love back onto their Maker, so that in the things that please you, you yourself not displease him. If souls please you, let them be loved in God, for they too are subject to change, but in him they stand firmly established — otherwise they would pass away and be gone. Let them be loved in him, then, and carry with you to him as many souls as you can, and say to them: "let us love him, let us love him: he made these things, and he is not far off. For he did not make them and then leave — they come from him and remain in him. See, there he is, wherever truth is loved. He is within the very heart, and yet the heart has strayed from him. Go back into your heart, you transgressors, and cling fast to the one who made you. Stand with him, and you will stand firm. Rest in him, and you will be at rest. Where are you going, down such rough roads? Where are you going? The good you love comes from him, but it is only good and pleasant through its connection to him, and it will rightly turn bitter, because it is unjust to love anything that comes from him, if he himself is abandoned for its sake. To what end, then, do you go on and on walking these difficult, exhausting roads? There is no rest where you are looking for it. Seek what you are seeking — but it is not there, where you are seeking it. You are seeking a blessed life in the land of death: it is not there. For how could there be a blessed life where there is no life at all?

"But our true Life came down here, and took on our death, and killed it, out of the abundance of his own life. And he thundered, calling loudly to us to return from here to him, into that hidden place he first came from into us, coming first into the Virgin's womb, where he was joined to our human nature, our mortal flesh, so that it would not remain mortal forever — and from there, like a bridegroom coming out of his wedding chamber, he rejoiced like a giant to run his course. For he did not linger, but ran, calling loudly through words, deeds, death, life, descent, ascension — crying out loudly to us to return to him. And he went out of our sight, so that we might return into our own heart, and find him there. For he departed, and yet, look — he is here. He would not stay long with us, yet he did not leave us; for he went away to the place he had never left, because the world was made by him. And he was in this world, and he came into this world to save sinners — my soul confesses to him, and he heals it, for it has sinned against him. You sons of men, how long will your hearts stay so slow? Even now, after Life has come down to you, will you not rise up and live? But where are you climbing to, when you are already up high and setting your mouth against the heavens? Come down, so that you may rise; rise to God. For you have fallen, by rising up against him." Tell them this, so that they may weep in the valley of tears, and so carry them up with you to God — because it is out of his spirit that you are speaking to them this way, if you speak at all, burning with the fire of love.

I knew none of this at the time, and I loved these lower beauties, and I was sinking down to the very bottom, and I said to my friends, "Do we love anything except what is beautiful? What, then, is the beautiful? And what is beauty? What is it that attracts us and wins us over to the things we love? For unless there were some grace and beauty in them, they could never draw us to them at all." And I noticed and understood that in bodies themselves there was one kind of beauty that came from their forming a sort of whole, and another kind that came from a fitting, mutual correspondence between parts — the way a part of the body relates to the whole, or a shoe fits a foot, and things like that. And this idea arose in my mind, straight out of my innermost heart, and I wrote "On the Fair and the Fitting" — two or three books, I think. You know, Lord, for it has slipped away from me; I no longer have them, they have gone astray from me, I don't know how.

But what moved me, Lord my God, to dedicate those books to Hierius — an orator of Rome I did not know by sight, but loved for the fame of his learning, which was outstanding in him, and for some words of his I had heard that pleased me? But he pleased me even more because he pleased others, who praised him highly, amazed that a Syrian, first trained in Greek eloquence, should afterward turn into a remarkable Latin orator, and one deeply learned in matters of philosophy besides. A man is praised, and, unseen, he is loved: does this love enter the hearer's heart out of the praiser's mouth? No — rather, one who loves kindles love in another. For that is how the one who is praised comes to be loved: when the one praising him is believed to be extolling him with a sincere heart — that is, when someone who loves him is the one praising him.

That is how I loved men then — by the judgment of men, not yours, my God, in whom no man is deceived. And yet, why not love someone for qualities like those of a famous charioteer, or a beast-fighter in the theater, known far and wide by cheap popularity — but instead in a very different way, and earnestly, in the way I wanted to be praised myself? For I did not want to be praised or loved the way actors are — though I myself did praise and love them — I would rather be unknown than known that way, and even hated than loved that way. Where, then, do these impulses toward such varied and different kinds of love lie stored up in one soul? Why, since we are equally men, do I love in another what, if I did not hate it, I would not spurn and cast away from myself? For it doesn't hold that, just as a good horse is loved by someone who would not want to be that horse even if he could, the same can be said of an actor, who shares our own nature. Do I then love in a man what I hate to be, when I myself am a man? Man himself is a great deep, whose very hairs you count, Lord, and not one of them falls to the ground without you. And yet the hairs of his head are easier to count than his feelings and the beats of his heart.

That orator was one of the sort I loved, wanting to be like him myself, and I went wrong through a swollen pride, tossed about by every wind — but steered by you, all the same, though very secretly. And how do I know, and how can I confidently confess to you, that I had loved him more because of the love of the men who praised him than for the very qualities he was praised for? Because if he had gone unpraised, and those same men had instead condemned him, and told the very same facts about him with scorn and contempt, I would never have been so kindled and stirred up to love him. And yet the facts would not have been any different, nor would he himself have been any different — only the feelings of the people reporting on him. See where the powerless soul lies, not yet held steady by the solidity of truth! Just as gusts of talk blow out of the chests of people who deal only in opinion, so the soul is carried this way and that, driven forward and back, and the light is clouded over for it, and the truth goes unseen. And look — it is right there in front of us. And it mattered a great deal to me that my speeches and my efforts should be known to that man: if he approved, I was all the more kindled; but if he disapproved, my empty heart, with none of your solidity in it, was wounded. And yet the "Fair and the Fitting," the book I wrote for him, I lingered over with pleasure, and surveyed it, and admired it, even though no one else shared in that admiration.

But I did not yet see what this weighty subject hinged on in your wisdom, you the almighty, who alone do wonders. My mind ranged through bodily forms, and I defined and distinguished "the fair," what is beautiful in itself, and "the fitting," whose beauty lies in its correspondence to something else — and I supported this with examples drawn from bodies. And I turned toward the nature of the mind, but the false notion I had of spiritual things kept me from seeing the truth. Yet the force of truth still flashed on its own into my eyes, and I turned my gasping soul away from bodiless substance toward outlines, colors, and bulky sizes. And since I could not see these things in the mind, I concluded I could not see my mind at all. And whereas in virtue I loved peace, and in vice I hated discord, in the one I noticed a unity, but in the other, a kind of division. And in that unity, I believed the rational soul consisted, and the nature of truth and of the highest good; but in that division, I imagined, wretchedly, that there was some unknown substance of irrational life, and the nature of the greatest evil — which I thought must be not only a substance but a living thing too, and yet not derived from you, my God, from whom all things come. And the first of these I called a Monad, as though it were a sexless soul; the second I called a Duad — anger in acts of violence, and lust in acts of depravity — not knowing what I was talking about. For I had not known or learned that evil is not a substance at all, nor is our soul that highest and unchangeable good.

For just as acts of violence arise when the emotion of the soul from which forceful action springs is corrupted, stirring itself up insolently and unrestrained; and lusts arise when the part of the soul that drinks in carnal pleasures is left ungoverned — so errors and false opinions pollute our conduct, if the reasoning soul itself is corrupted. That was my condition then: I did not know that the soul must be lit by another light in order to share in truth, since it is not itself the nature of truth. For you will light my lamp, Lord my God, you will light up my darkness; and we have all received out of your fullness, for you are the true light that lights every man who comes into the world; for in you there is no changeableness, not even a shadow of change.

But I pressed toward you, and was thrust back from you, so that I might get a taste of death — for you resist the proud. But what could be prouder than for me, with a strange kind of madness, to insist that I was by nature what you are? For whereas I was subject to change — this much was obvious to me, since my very wish to become wise was a wish to go from worse to better — I still chose instead to imagine you as subject to change, rather than admit that I myself was not what you are. So I was pushed back by you, and you resisted my useless stubbornness, and I pictured bodily shapes, and, being flesh myself, I accused flesh; and, a wind that blows past and vanishes, I did not return to you, but wandered on and on toward things that have no being — not in you, not in me, not in any body. Nor were they created for me by your truth, but devised out of my own emptiness, out of bodily things. And I used to ask your faithful little ones, my fellow citizens — from whom, without knowing it myself, I stood in exile — I used to ask them, chattering foolishly, "Why then does the soul, which God created, go wrong?" But I did not want to be asked in return, "Why then does God go wrong?" And I insisted that your unchangeable substance was forced into error, rather than admit that my own changeable substance had wandered off by its own choice and now, as punishment, lay in error.

I was some twenty-six or twenty-seven years old when I wrote those books, turning over in myself fictions built out of bodies, buzzing in the ears of my heart, which I turned, sweet truth, toward your inward melody, meditating on "the fair and the fitting," longing to stand still and listen to you, and to rejoice greatly at the Bridegroom's voice — but I could not; the voices of my own errors kept hurrying me off outward, and under the weight of my own pride I was sinking into the lowest pit. For you did not let me hear joy and gladness, and the bones that had not yet been humbled did not exult.

And what good did it do me that, barely twenty years old, a book of Aristotle's fell into my hands — the one they call the Ten Categories, on whose very name I hung as on something great and divine, every time my rhetoric teacher in Carthage, and others reckoned learned, mouthed it with cheeks puffed up with pride — and that I read and understood it on my own, without help? And when I compared notes with others, who said they had barely understood it even with highly capable tutors — teachers who not only explained it aloud but drew many things out in the sand — they could tell me no more about it than I had already learned reading it by myself. The book seemed to me to speak very clearly about substances, such as "man," and about their qualities — the shape of a man, and what kind it is; his height, how many feet tall; his relationship, whose brother he is; or where he is placed; or when he was born; or whether he is standing or sitting; or whether he is shod or armed; or whether he does something or has something done to him — and all the countless other things that might fall under these nine Categories, of which I have given a few examples, or under that chief Category of Substance.

What good did all this do me, when it even got in my way? For imagining that whatever existed must fall under those ten Categories, I tried, in that same manner, to understand even your wonderful and unchangeable Unity, my God, as though you too were subject to your own greatness or beauty, so that — as with bodies — these would exist in you as in some underlying subject; when really you yourself are your own greatness and beauty. A body, by contrast, is not great or beautiful simply by being a body, since even if it were less great or less beautiful, it would still be a body. But what I conceived of you was falsehood, not truth — fictions born of my own misery, not the realities of your blessedness. For you had commanded, and it was carried out in me, that the earth should bring forth briars and thorns for me, and that I should eat my bread by the sweat of my brow.

And what good did it do me that I, a vile slave to vile passions, read on my own and understood all the books I could get hold of on the so-called liberal arts? I took delight in them, but I did not know where all the true or certain things in them came from. For I had my back turned to the light and my face turned toward the things it lit up, so that my face, with which I made out the things illuminated, was itself not illuminated. Whatever was written on rhetoric, or logic, geometry, music, or arithmetic, I understood by myself without much trouble and without any teacher — you know this, Lord my God, because both quickness of understanding and sharpness in discerning are your gifts — yet I did not for that reason offer any sacrifice to you. So it did not serve my good, but rather my ruin, since I went about trying to keep so good a portion of my inheritance under my own control, and I did not keep my strength for you, but wandered away from you into a far country, to spend it on prostitutes. For what good were fine abilities to me, when they were not put to good use? I did not realize that these subjects were reached only with great difficulty, even by the studious and talented, until I tried explaining them to others — when the one who most excelled at them was the one who did not lag too far behind me.

But what good did it do me to imagine that you, Lord God, the Truth, were some vast, bright body, and I a fragment of that body? Too great a perversity! But that is what I was. Yet I am not ashamed, my God, to confess your mercies toward me, and to call on you — I who was not ashamed then to declare my blasphemies to men, and to bark against you. What good did my nimble wit do me then, in those subjects, and in all those tangled volumes I untangled without any human teacher's help, when I was going so badly wrong, with such sacrilegious shamelessness, in the teaching that concerns piety? Or what harm was a far slower wit to your little ones, since they did not wander far from you, so that in the nest of your Church they might be safely fledged, and nourish the wings of love on the food of a sound faith? Lord our God, let us hope under the shadow of your wings; protect us, and carry us. You will carry us both when we are small, and you will carry us even to gray hairs, for when our firmness is you, it is real firmness, but when it is our own, it is only weakness. Our good always lives with you, and when we turn away from it, we are turned aside. Let us now, Lord, return, so that we are not overturned, because with you our good lives without any decay — and that good is you. Nor do we need to fear that there will be no place to return to, because we fell away from it — for through our absence, our home did not fall: your eternity.
